title: Where data comes from: files, APIs, databases, scraping
story:
Four ways to get data, and the useful thing to notice is not that they differ in difficulty. A file is the easiest and a scrape is the hardest, and that ranking tells you almost nothing worth knowing. What separates them is who can change the data under you, and what you are permitted to do with it.

A file is frozen. That is its virtue and its lie: it was true at some moment nobody wrote down, and it will go on looking current for years. An API is a contract, and the other party can revise it — a field renamed, a page size changed, a rate limit introduced overnight. A database is the closest thing to the truth, but it is shaped for the application that writes to it rather than for the question you are asking, and your read competes with that application for the same machine. And a scrape is the one source that never agreed to be a source at all.

That last one is worth being precise about, because the received version of the law is wrong in both directions. The case everybody cites is hiQ Labs against LinkedIn, and the received version is that the Ninth Circuit ruled scraping public data legal. What the panel actually said was narrower: that hiQ had raised a serious question as to whether the without authorization concept in the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act applies where prior authorization is not generally required but a particular person, or bot, is refused access. It affirmed a preliminary injunction and remanded for further proceedings. A serious question at the injunction stage is not a final holding.

Then hiQ lost anyway. In November 2022 the district court found it had breached the user agreement by scraping and by creating fake accounts, and in December the parties filed a consent judgment: 500,000 dollars, a permanent injunction against further scraping, and deletion of the profile data and of the code written to reach it. The statute and the contract were two different questions the whole time, and winning the famous one did not answer the other. Note that because those conclusions were stipulated rather than found, they set no precedent either.

The convention that governs the polite version of the same activity took twenty-eight years to be written down. Koster defined the Robots Exclusion Protocol in 1994 and it became a standards track document only in 2022 — and that document is careful to say it is not a substitute for content security, because listing a path in the file tells the world the path exists. Everything in this track rests on knowing which of these four you are holding, when it was captured, and who else can move it.

problem.name: Provenance
problem.shape: The data you need lives somewhere you do not control, and you are about to make a copy of it and then reason about the copy.
tell: the analysis is as of a date that nobody chose deliberately
the loader has no handling for a second page of results
the figures reconcile against nothing, because there is nothing to reconcile them against
permission was never considered, because the data was reachable
problem.move: Name the source of record before writing the loader. Record, next to the data itself, when it was captured, who can change it, and what you are permitted to do with it. Then make the loader assert the shape it expects, so that a renamed column stops the pipeline instead of quietly becoming a column of nulls.
problem.invariant: Every row you hold is a copy of something that was true somewhere at some instant, and the copy does not update itself. Capture time and owner are properties of the data, not metadata about the project.
problem.breaks: The assertion catches changes in shape, and shape is only half of it. A source can go on returning the same columns while the meaning behind one of them changes — a status code reused, a currency switched, a field that used to be populated quietly going empty. Nothing in the pipeline can see that; only reconciliation against an independent figure can.

cost.time: a schema assertion and a capture timestamp per source, written once and paid back the first time something upstream moves
cost.space: the capture time and the source identifier stored alongside the rows, which is a column or two
cost.beats: discovering the change from the model's output, which is the same information arriving weeks later with a training run attached to it

worked.problem: Is it legal to scrape publicly available data? The case everyone cites says yes.
worked.reasoning:
It depends which law you mean, and that is the answer rather than a dodge.

Under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, the Ninth Circuit's panel found hiQ had raised a serious question as to whether accessing a public profile is access without authorization at all. The statute's language presumes a baseline where permission is ordinarily required; a page served to anyone who asks does not obviously sit on that baseline. But note what the court did with that finding: it affirmed a preliminary injunction and sent the case back. It did not hold that scraping is lawful.

Under contract, hiQ lost. The user agreement prohibited scraping, hiQ had agreed to it, and it had also created fake accounts — so in November 2022 the district court found a breach, and in December the parties stipulated to a judgment of 500,000 dollars, a permanent injunction, and deletion of both the data and the code that fetched it.

So the same conduct was arguably not a federal computer crime and was still a breach of contract with a company-ending remedy attached. Those were never the same question. The shorthand answer — scraping public data is legal, hiQ won — gets the statute roughly right, the outcome exactly wrong, and the distinction entirely missing.

Two further cautions. The consent judgment was stipulated by the parties rather than found by the court, so it is not precedent for anyone else. And none of this is the whole field: terms of service, copyright, database rights and data protection law all sit alongside, and they vary by jurisdiction in a way a single appellate opinion does not settle.

What a practitioner should take from it is procedural rather than legal. Before scraping, read the terms you have accepted, check the exclusion file, do not create accounts to get past a login, and keep a record of what you took and when — because the question that ended hiQ was never about the statute.

  FILE        frozen. no expiry date anywhere in it.
              fails by:  being silently old
              ask:       captured when? by whom?

  API         a contract the other side can revise.
              fails by:  page 1 of 8, rate limits,
                         a field renamed overnight
              ask:       what is the pagination?
                         what is the limit?

  DATABASE    true, but shaped for the app that
              writes to it, not for your question.
              fails by:  answering about NOW while
                         you treat it as THEN;
                         your read competing with
                         production traffic
              ask:       read replica? as-of column?

  SCRAPE      the only source that never agreed.
              fails by:  parsing on after the layout
                         changed; and by contract law
              ask:       terms? exclusion file?
                         am I making an account?

     statute and contract are two questions.

problem.practice: Take a dataset you are currently using. Write down four things: where it came from, the moment it was captured, who can change it without telling you, and what permits you to hold it. If you cannot answer all four, you have found the interesting problem. Then rename a column in the source and see how far into your pipeline the change travels before anything complains.

beats.broke: The data a model needs lives somewhere you do not control, and the four usual ways of getting it are not four levels of difficulty — they are four different arrangements with whoever holds it.
beats.fix: Classify a source by who can change it and by what you are permitted to do with it. A file is frozen, an API is a contract the other side can revise, a database is shaped for the application that writes to it rather than for your question, and a scrape is the only source that never agreed to be one.
beats.cost: All four fail silently at read time. The file carries no expiry date, the API returns the first page of eight, the database answers a question about now that you will read as a question about then, and the scrape keeps parsing after the layout has changed.

interview.q: Is it legal to scrape publicly available data? The case everyone cites says yes.
interview.trap: Answering with the headline — the Ninth Circuit ruled for hiQ, so scraping public data is legal. That conflates a preliminary injunction with a holding, and it ignores that the company which won that ruling was permanently enjoined and paid damages under a different body of law.
interview.answer:
It depends which law, and the distinction is the whole answer.

Under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, the Ninth Circuit panel found that hiQ had raised a serious question as to whether reading a publicly served profile is access without authorization at all — the statute's wording presumes a baseline where permission is ordinarily required, and a page handed to anyone who asks does not sit on that baseline. But the panel affirmed a preliminary injunction and remanded. That is not a holding that scraping is lawful, and it gets quoted as though it were.

Under contract, hiQ lost outright. It had accepted a user agreement prohibiting scraping, and it had created fake accounts. The district court found a breach in November 2022, and in December the parties stipulated to 500,000 dollars, a permanent injunction against further scraping, and deletion of both the member data and the code that collected it.

So the same conduct was arguably not a federal computer crime and was still a contract breach that ended the company. Those were always two questions, and the popular summary answers the less consequential one.

Two caveats I would add unprompted. The consent judgment was stipulated rather than found, so it binds nobody else. And the statute is not the field: terms of service, copyright, database rights and data protection all apply alongside it and vary by jurisdiction.

In practice the useful posture is procedural. Read the terms you have accepted, honour the exclusion file, never create an account to get past a login, and keep a record of what you took and when — because what ended hiQ was never the statute.

THE FOUR, RANKED BY WHAT YOU CONTROL

   file      <- you control the copy, not the truth
   API       <- they control the contract

THE CASE, IN ONE LINE

   won the statute, lost the contract,
   $500,000 and a permanent injunction.
takeaway: A source is defined by who can change it and what you may do with it, not by how hard it is to read — and every row you hold is a copy of something true somewhere at an instant you should have written down.
